newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila shares dive, C.Bank acts on property scares.
newsitem.headline: Manila shares dive, C.Bank acts on property scares.

text.p: Waves of selling sent Philippines shares tumbling five percent to their lowest levels in two years on Tuesday, and analysts warned the future looked bleak for a market now dominated by fears of a property slump.

Apparently taking fright itself over the ferocity of the attack on shares, the Philippines Central Bank announced just after the market closed that it was imposing its first ever limit on the amount banks could lend real estate companies.
Tuesday's market fall was the biggest one-day drop in 26 months.

"It's not just bloodletting, this is a massacre," said research director Henry Ong of Sapphire Securities as the Philippine Stock Exchange key index fell 128.7 points, or 4.54 percent, to 2,708.44 points.
The day's worst losers included property firms Ayala Land Inc, Empire East Land Holdings Inc and Filinvest Land, which all fell a little more than seven percent.

Uncurbed fears of a property bust similar to that in Thailand helped unsettle the market despite repeated official assurances that the loan exposures to real estate firms were well within tolerable limits, analysts said.
But two hours after the market had shut on Tuesday, the Central Bank told banks that no more than 20 percent of their loans could go to property firms.
Those already over the limit have one year to comply.
Bank governor Gabriel Singson also cut the amount banks could lend to 60 percent from 70 percent of a property's value.
The two measures were "designed to prevent banks from overlending to the real estate sector that could undermine the country's financial system," he said.

"It is very obvious that people are worried about it. This is a good way to reassure the people, especially the armchair analysts," Johnny Noe Ravalo, chief economist of the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP), told Reuters.

Though the quality of bank loans has not been proven to be deteriorating, the measures should calm lingering concerns over the possibility of a repeat of the Thailand banking crisis in the Philippines, he said.
But a leading economist from a domestic commercial bank said the measures were unnecessary since individual banks had their own internal risk management controls.
"Any policy that will curtail banking activity is counterproductive," he said.
He said drawing parallels with Thailand was unfair.
"We had been tipped as the next Mexico when the Mexico debacle happened, but we were able to survive it."
Analysts predicted, however, that the share market would continue to drop.
"It's like a giant stone falling. You just don't stop it," said Irving Ackerman, president of I. Ackerman & Co.
"I can't remember a drop like this for a long time," he said. "It's still a little bit grim. For the time being we just have to grit our teeth."
Analysts saw little chance of a quick recovery.
"We are seeing end-of-cycle delirium. This is the first phase of the correction," said SBC Warburg analyst Joey Salceda.
"The cleansing process has just started. There is too much froth," he said.
The battering of the bourse also unnerved the currency market. Traders said the drop would put pressure on the Philippine peso and could force the Central Bank to hike interest rates.
At 0930 GMT, the peso was quoted lower at 26.369/370 to the U.S. dollar, against its opening at 26.366 and its previous close at 26.367.
